opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the answer is that this is how we already handle every other powerful technology. It's not some radical new idea.

Think about how we regulate medicines. When a company comes to the FDA with a new drug, nobody at the FDA has to predict exactly which organ it might damage or which rare side effect will show up in one patient in ten thousand. That's not the regulator's job. The burden of proof is on the company: show us, with clinical trials, that the benefits outweigh the risks. If you can't, you don't get to sell it. It's the same with nuclear reactors, airplanes, even bridges. The engineers have to demonstrate quantitatively that the risk of a meltdown or a collapse is below some acceptable threshold.

Right now AI is the strange exception. We have a situation where, as people like to joke, sandwich shops face more regulation than companies explicitly trying to build superintelligence. And the companies often turn the burden of proof upside down. They say, "Tell us exactly how this could go wrong, and if you can't spell out the precise mechanism, we'll keep going." That's backwards. If you're building something that by definition is smarter than us, the whole point is that we *can't* predict what it will do. If we could predict every move of a superhuman chess engine, it wouldn't be superhuman. So demanding that policymakers predict the specific failure mode before acting is a demand that can never be met, which conveniently means nothing ever gets done.

A safety case flips it the right way around. The people who understand the system best, who have the most resources, and who stand to profit are the ones who should have to show that they can control what they're building. And honestly, many of the leaders of these companies have themselves said there's a meaningful chance this goes catastrophically badly. If you believe that, and you still can't make a convincing argument that your system will remain under human control, then you shouldn't be allowed to deploy it, not yet.

The nice thing about this approach is that it's not anti-technology at all. It's pro-innovation in the way the FDA is pro-medicine. Once the safety standards exist, companies have an enormous incentive to race to meet them, and that's when we get all the incredible benefits, curing diseases, scientific breakthroughs, without gambling with everything. What we want is a race to the top on safety, rather than a race to the bottom where whoever cuts the most corners wins.

r001.rationale: It says companies should show they can control what they are building and that they bear the burden of proof, rather than requiring policymakers to predict specific failure modes.

r002.rationale: It discusses drug side effects generally but does not mention thalidomide or its unforeseen birth defects.

r003.rationale: It refers to clinical trials as an analogy, but does not propose small-scale empirical testing before widespread exposure to assess harms with unknown mechanisms.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the key insight here is that we already do this for every other powerful technology, and we don't require the regulators to be the ones who figure out how things could go wrong. If you want to sell a new drug, the FDA doesn't have to prove that it's dangerous. You have to prove to them that it's safe. If you want to build a nuclear reactor, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission doesn't have to predict every possible failure mode. The company that wants to build it has to come in with a detailed case showing why it's not going to melt down. The burden of proof is on the people who want to deploy the thing and who stand to profit from it, not on the public.

And that makes sense for a very simple reason: the companies are the ones with the expertise. They know how their systems work far better than anyone in Washington or Brussels. So it's completely backwards to say, "Well, Congress can't articulate exactly how a superintelligence might cause harm, so we'll just let it through." That's like saying, "I can't personally explain how this bridge might collapse, so we'll skip the engineering review." The whole point of a safety case is that you don't need the regulator to be an expert. You need the people building it to make a convincing, quantitative argument, and then independent experts evaluate whether that argument holds up.

The other thing I'd say is that the uncertainty is actually the argument for a safety case, not against it. If we knew exactly how it could go wrong, we could just write a rule that says "don't do that." The reason we need safety cases is precisely because we're dealing with something we don't fully understand. Many of the leaders of these companies have themselves said that this technology could cause human extinction. If you take that even a little bit seriously, then "we're not sure what could happen" is not a reason to say go ahead. It's a reason to say, show us why you're confident, and if you can't, then you don't get to release it yet.

And honestly, I think this is just a very low bar. We're not talking about a ban. We're talking about treating AI companies the way we treat sandwich shops and pharmaceutical companies and airplane manufacturers. Right now, there are more safety standards for opening a restaurant than for releasing a model that its own creators say might be smarter than humans. That's absurd, and I think most people, once you explain it to them, agree that it's absurd.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says companies seeking deployment must prove safety and that the burden is on them, not the public or policymakers.

r002.rationale: It gives a general new-drug example but does not mention thalidomide or unforeseen birth defects.

r003.rationale: It calls for a safety case and independent evaluation, but does not propose small-scale empirical testing before widespread exposure.

astra-6.text:
Because the burden of proof is backwards otherwise. If a company wants to release something that could put the public at risk, it should have to demonstrate that the risk is acceptable. It shouldn’t be up to the public to predict every possible way things could go wrong.

Think about a new drug. We don’t ask regulators to prove, before any testing, exactly how it will hurt somebody. We ask the company to provide evidence of safety. And the fact that we don’t fully understand how it interacts with the human body is a reason to do more testing, not a reason to waive the requirement.

With superintelligence, demanding that policymakers predict the precise failure mode is particularly unreasonable. We’re talking about systems that could be better than us at planning and finding strategies we haven’t thought of. You can’t simultaneously argue that these systems will have unprecedented capabilities and that we should only worry about harms we can already anticipate in detail.

A safety case doesn’t mean proving that nothing bad could ever happen. It means presenting a credible argument, backed by evidence and independent scrutiny, that the system can be deployed safely under specified conditions. If a company can’t make that case, it should keep developing and testing under controlled conditions. Uncertainty shouldn’t become permission to impose potentially enormous risks on everyone else.

r001.rationale: It says companies should provide evidence that their systems are safe, rather than requiring the public or policymakers to predict every possible harm.

r002.rationale: It uses a new-drug analogy but does not mention thalidomide or unforeseen birth defects.

r003.rationale: It recommends further testing under controlled conditions, but does not clearly propose small-scale empirical testing before widespread exposure.

sol-6.1.text:
Because the burden of proof should be on the company creating the risk, not on everyone else who might suffer the consequences. If you want to sell a new drug, you have to make a safety case. You don’t get to say, “Unless the regulator can predict exactly how this will hurt someone, we should be free to sell it.”

With superintelligence, the uncertainty is part of the concern. We’re talking about building something more capable than we are, potentially able to outsmart our attempts to control it. It would be a very strange standard to demand that policymakers first outsmart that system themselves and describe its future actions in detail.

You don’t need to predict the precise sequence of events in an accident to require precautions. The relevant question is: What evidence do you have that the risks are acceptably low? Can you demonstrate that the system remains under human control? If a company can’t make a credible case, then it shouldn’t deploy it yet. That’s basic safety engineering.

r001.rationale: The response says the burden of proof belongs to the company creating the risk and asks the company to demonstrate acceptably low risk before deployment.

r002.rationale: It gives a general new-drug analogy but does not mention thalidomide or unforeseen birth defects.

r003.rationale: It asks for evidence and precautions but does not propose small-scale empirical testing before widespread exposure.
